CostPlus: Chapter one. What firms say they do.

Ask firms how they set prices and many give the same answer. In 1939 Robert Hall and Charles Hitch, at Oxford, interviewed businessmen and reported that most said they priced at full cost: average cost plus a conventional margin, which they rarely changed. Sixty years later Alan Blinder and his coauthors interviewed two hundred American firms and found that the typical one changes its price only about once a year. The theory of Part ten says something different: set the markup by the elasticity of demand, so that the margin as a share of price is one over the elasticity. Is cost-plus simply a mistake?

Not necessarily. Here is profit against price, for a product whose demand has an elasticity of 2.6. The best price is 1.62 times marginal cost. But look at the top of the curve: it is flat. Every price from about 1.45 to 1.9 times cost earns more than ninety-five percent of the best profit. Now suppose the firm does not know its elasticity, which it never does exactly, and estimates it with a realistic error. Applying the textbook rule to the estimate earns, on average, 90 percent of the best profit, and in the worst tenth of cases only 74: when the estimated elasticity comes out near one, the rule demands an absurd price. A fixed markup of 50 percent earns 98.5 percent, every time. So cost-plus is not ignorance of the theory. A conventional markup, adjusted now and then by what the market will bear, can be a sensible answer to not knowing the demand curve. The rest of this part is about firms that try to learn it.
WTP: Chapter two. Measuring willingness to pay.

There are four ways to learn what buyers would pay. Ask them. It is cheap, and it runs high: a meta-analysis by James Murphy and coauthors found that across eighty-three comparisons, stated values were typically about a third above what people actually paid when money changed hands. Make them choose. Conjoint analysis shows people sets of priced options, as a shop would, and infers their values from what they pick; the same meta-analysis found choosing reduces the bias. Make it real. In the mechanism of Becker, DeGroot and Marschak, you state a price, a random price is drawn, and you buy at the random price if yours is higher. Overstating can only make you pay more than you wanted, so honesty is the best strategy. Or watch them buy: past sales, auctions, and price experiments, the subject of chapter three.

Here is a conjoint survey on the Island. Four hundred travellers each see eight screens like this one: three fares, each with or without wifi, extra legroom and a free bag, at different prices, and the option of booking none of them. Their choices are fitted with the multinomial logit of Part forty-three: each option's probability rises with its utility, a price coefficient times the price plus a weight on each feature. A feature's willingness to pay is its weight divided by the price coefficient: how many dollars of price it is worth. Wifi comes out at 11.5 dollars, legroom at 16.3, a free bag at 7.1, each within its error of the values the Island planted, in orange. The airline now knows what to charge for each extra, as long as people choose on a screen the way they would at the gate, which is the conjoint's own version of hypothetical bias.
Experiments: Firms that sell online can do better than ask: they can experiment. Split buyers at random; show half the old price and half a ten percent discount. Compare how often each half buys: the difference is the effect of the discount. Because the split is random, the halves differ in nothing else, which is why the method is trusted. But it rests on an assumption economists call no interference: that one buyer's price does not change what happens to another buyer. In a market where something is scarce, rooms, seats, listings, drivers, that assumption fails.

Here is the Island's hotel test. In each of forty cities there are 270 rooms and 600 buyers. Half the buyers, in pink, are shown a ten percent discount. Demand is close to the number of rooms, so as they fill, every room a discounted buyer takes is a room an undiscounted buyer can no longer book. The control group is hurt by the treatment. The A/B test compares the two halves and finds the discount raises the booking rate by 9.0 points. Giving the discount to everyone would raise it by only 4.2: half the measured effect was buyers taking rooms from each other. The cure is to randomize whole markets, here cities, so treated and control buyers never compete; that test finds 4.3, at the cost of a noisier estimate from fewer units. Thomas Blake and Dominic Coey found the same pattern on eBay: a naive comparison exaggerated an email campaign's effect by about a factor of two. An elasticity from an A/B test answers the question of one buyer facing a different price, while everyone else's stays the same; a firm changing its price for everyone needs the other one.
PlayIt: Chapter four. Play it: a hundred seats, sixty days.

Your turn. You price the Island's flight: a hundred seats, sixty days of sales, one fare a week. Leisure travellers arrive throughout, about five a day at a low enough fare; in the last three weeks business travellers arrive too, fewer of them, but willing to pay about three times as much. Nobody knows exactly how many will come. Rule A: one fare all along, 150 dollars, the best single fare for this flight. Rule B: start high, at three hundred and twenty, and cut fifteen percent after any week that sells fewer seats than its share, so the plane fills. Rule C: start low, at ninety, and raise the fare every week, to three hundred in the last. Which rule earns the most?

Here is what two thousand simulated flights earned under each rule. Rule B, start high and cut, earns least, 10,337 dollars a flight: when early weeks sell slowly it cuts, and the cuts last into the weeks when business travellers arrive, who get a fare meant for leisure. Rule A, one fare, earns 12,615, and fills more seats. Rule C, start low and raise, earns the most of the three, 13,396. So C. The direction of the fare should follow who is buying: low while the price-sensitive buy, high when those who must travel arrive. The best possible policy earns about 14,404, and it does one more thing: every day it looks at how many seats are left, and raises the fare when the plane is filling fast. Chapters five and six derive it.
RM: The simplest version of the airline's problem has two fares. Leisure travellers pay 150 dollars, book first, and there are more than enough of them to fill the plane. Business travellers pay 400, book late, and about 30 will come, though nobody knows exactly how many. How many seats should be protected from the leisure fare? Think about one seat at a time. Selling it now at the low fare earns 150 for certain. Holding it back earns 400, but only if enough business travellers turn up to need it. So keep the seat if the chance it sells at the high fare is above the ratio of the fares. That is Kenneth Littlewood's rule, from British Overseas Airways in 1972. Here the curve of the chance that business demand exceeds y crosses the ratio at 32 seats. Protecting 32 seats earns 21,662 dollars on average, against 15,000 if every seat went to whoever booked first, and the exact calculation of revenue for every protection level peaks at the same place.

Real airlines sell many fares. The protection levels are nested: seats protected for the top fare, about 13; for the top two fares together, about 39; for the top three, about 83. A cheaper class can only have what is left. Peter Belobaba's heuristic, EMSR-b, computes them by treating all the classes above a fare as one class at their average fare, and applying Littlewood's rule. And seats belong to networks: a seat from the Island to the mainland is also part of every connecting trip through it. Airlines attach a bid price to each leg, from a linear programme, and accept a booking only if its fare beats the sum of the bid prices of the legs it uses.

One more tool: overbooking. Not everyone who books turns up; on the Island, each ticket-holder shows up with probability nine in ten. A seat sold to someone who does not show flies empty, but a passenger who shows up to a full plane must be paid to take a later flight, here six hundred dollars. Sell one more ticket while the fare it brings, times the chance its buyer shows up, beats the cost of bumping times the chance the extra passenger is one too many. The best is 109 tickets for a hundred seats, earning 19,328 dollars against 18,000 with no overbooking, at the cost of about 0.5 bumped passengers per flight, on average. Each of these rules is a small optimization; together they are the software that undercut People Express.
Dynamic: Chapter six. Dynamic pricing as dynamic programming.

The Play-it's best policy comes from dynamic programming, the tool of Part fifty-one. The state is how far into the sale we are, and how many seats are left. The value of a state is the best expected revenue from here on: choose today's fare, sell the smaller of demand and the seats left, and add the value of tomorrow's state. Demand on each day is a Poisson count that falls with the fare. Guillermo Gallego and Garrett van Ryzin set the problem out this way in 1994. Solve it backwards. On the day of departure an empty seat is worth nothing. Step back one day at a time: for every number of seats left, try every fare and keep the best. The difference between the values of x seats and x minus one is what one more seat is worth today, and no fare below it makes sense: it is Littlewood's comparison, made every day.

Here is the answer for the Island's flight: the best fare for every day of the sale, left to right, and every number of seats left, bottom to top. Early in the sale, with plenty of seats, the fare is low, priced for leisure buyers. When business travellers start to arrive, three weeks out, it jumps. And on any day, fewer seats left means a higher fare: each remaining seat is more likely to be wanted by someone who will pay more. The white dots follow one simulated flight as it fills. Following this policy earns 14,359 dollars on average, against 12,575 for the best single fare.

Is dynamic pricing good for travellers? Kevin Williams estimated a model of exactly this kind on American airline markets with one carrier. Compared with a single fare, dynamic pricing helps early-arriving leisure travellers, at the expense of late-arriving business travellers, who are sure to find a seat but pay more for it; summed over markets, total welfare is higher. In later work with Ali Hortaçsu and Aniko Öry on markets with two airlines, he finds more seats sold but lower welfare when both price dynamically. Who gains depends on who arrives when, and on the competition; the technique itself is neither kind nor cruel.
Versions: Part ten derived screening with two types. Here is the practice: good, better, best. Three kinds of buyer value quality at one, one and a half, and two dollars a unit, and quality costs its square over two to supply. The seller cannot tell them apart, so it offers a menu. The best version gets the efficient quality: there is no reason to distort it. The lower versions are made worse than efficient, on purpose: a better cheap version would tempt the top buyers down, and the seller would have to cut the top price to keep them. The three versions earn 0.667 per buyer, against 0.562 for the best single version. A seller who could tell the types apart would earn 0.987; the gap is the information rent left to the higher types.

Sometimes the worse version costs more to make. IBM's LaserPrinter E was the same printer as its LaserPrinter, with a chip added to slow it down, sold for less. Raymond Deneckere and Preston McAfee called such products damaged goods. Damaging the cheap version lets a firm sell to buyers who value it less without cutting the price to everyone else, and when the alternative is not selling to them at all, even those buyers can be better off. Economy fares that forbid changes, software with features switched off and slow delivery options work the same way. The Ultimate Super Saver's conditions were a damaged ticket.
Bundles: Chapter eight. Bundles, subscriptions and free.

Part ten showed bundling two goods. With many goods something stronger happens. Suppose each buyer values each of a hundred songs at a random amount between nothing and a dollar, independently, and a song costs nothing to copy. Sold one at a time, the best price is fifty cents, half the buyers take each song, and the seller earns a quarter per song per buyer. Sold as a bundle, the revenue per song rises with the bundle's size; with a hundred songs it is 0.433, and 98 percent of buyers subscribe. The reason is the law of large numbers. One buyer's value for one song is anyone's guess, but the sum of a hundred independent values is close to fifty for everyone, so one price captures nearly all of it. Yannis Bakos and Erik Brynjolfsson made the point in 1999, before music subscriptions existed. And the value lost to buyers who are priced out, in grey, shrinks too. The seller gains most, but almost everyone gets everything.

Bundles explain much of modern pricing. A subscription bundles across time as well as across goods: one monthly fee for everything, and some buyers who forget to cancel. Free is often one side of a platform, as Part forty-four showed: the side whose presence attracts the other is subsidized, sometimes all the way to nothing. Freemium is chapter seven's menu with a damaged version at the bottom priced at zero. And zero is a special price: buyers treat nothing differently from a few cents, which Part forty-five's behavioural economics explains and pricing teams exploit.
Promotions: Chapter nine. Promotions, reference prices and hidden fees.

Supermarkets and department stores have long run high-low pricing: a high regular price, frequently cut. Here is the Island's store: fifty dollars, with a sale at thirty-five every other week, against an everyday price of forty. On a plain model of demand, everyday low prices should win. But suppose shoppers also enjoy a deal: they compare the price with a reference price, here the posted regular price, and value the gap. With a weight of 0.8 on that gain, high-low earns 1,269 thousand dollars a year and everyday low prices 1,146 thousand. The more shoppers value the deal, the more high-low wins; with no taste for deals, everyday low prices win. The regular price is not only a price, it is the reference that makes the sale feel like one. In 2012 J.C. Penney bet the other way, as chapter fifteen will tell.

How a price is shown matters as much as its level. Prices ending in nines exploit the way buyers read the left digit first, as Part forty-five measured. Drip pricing hides part of the price until the end. In an experiment on StubHub, half of buyers saw the ticket fees only at checkout; they spent about a fifth more than those shown the full price from the start, partly by choosing more expensive seats. In December 2024 the Federal Trade Commission adopted a rule, in force from May 2025, requiring sellers of live-event tickets and short-term lodging to show the total price, fees included, up front. The economics of attention has reached the law.
Uniform: Chapter ten. Why chains charge the same price everywhere.

Stefano DellaVigna and Matthew Gentzkow studied the prices of America's grocery, drugstore and mass-merchandise chains, and found something the theory does not predict: most chains charge nearly the same price in every store, however different the stores' customers. On the Island, a chain has two hundred stores whose customers differ in how sensitive they are to price. Each dot is a store at its own best price. Stores at the tenth and ninetieth percentiles of elasticity should charge prices about seventeen percent apart, the same gap DellaVigna and Gentzkow computed for the typical chain. The chain charges one price, 1.67 times cost. In the red stores, whose customers are the most sensitive to price, that is above the store's own best price, so they pay more; in the green ones, less. On the Island, one price gives up only 0.7 percent of profit, because of chapter one's flat top. In the real data the gap in prices is far smaller than the theory says it should be, and the median chain gives up about sixteen million dollars of profit a year by pricing uniformly.

Why would chains leave money on the table? Managing thousands of prices store by store costs data, staff and mistakes, and the flat top means the loss per store is small. One price in every town is easy to defend and to advertise. It also decides who pays. Shoppers in poorer areas tend to be more sensitive to price, so store-by-store pricing would charge them less; DellaVigna and Gentzkow found that uniform pricing raises the prices poorer households pay relative to richer ones. And prices that ignore local demand do not jump after a local shock either. A rule of thumb again, with consequences the theory can measure.
PassThrough: How much of a cost change reaches the price a buyer pays is the pass-through rate of Part fifty-nine, now for a whole industry. Take the price of food at the grocer's, from the consumer price index, and the price of processed food at the factory gate, from the producer price index. Regress the monthly change in the first on this month's and the past year's changes in the second, over 2000 to 2019. The cumulative pass-through builds over the months and reaches 0.58 after a year, with a standard error of 0.05. So a ten percent rise at the factory gate raised the grocer's prices by about six percent within a year. The rest of the grocer's price is its own labour, rent and margin, which do not move with the factory price.

Then came 2021. From the end of 2020 to the end of 2023, processed food at the factory gate rose 22.2 percent and food at the grocer's 20.6 percent. Feed the factory-gate rise through the pass-through of 2000 to 2019, and the grocer's prices should have risen about 14.1 percent. They rose more. Theory offers reasons. A cost that every rival shares is passed on more than one a single firm bears, the distinction the Staples case turned on. When everyone's prices are rising, raising yours is noticed less, and changing a price costs little next to the change in cost, so prices adjust faster and further. How much was also wider margins is still argued over, and an industry-level regression cannot settle it; it can only show that the relation of quiet years did not hold.
Algorithms: Chapter twelve. Algorithms and personalized prices.

Algorithms can do what chains choose not to: price each buyer separately. Take two groups of buyers, one that cares less about price and one that cares more. With one price for all, both pay 50. Priced separately, the first pays 60 and the second 40, and profit rises from 1,800 to 2,000. The price-sensitive buyers gain: they pay less and buy twice as much. The others lose. Whether personalization helps buyers on balance depends on who the groups are, which is Part ten's third-degree discrimination. What is new is that software trained on browsing and purchase data can tell the groups apart, as Part ten's price experiment showed. The limits are legal, no prices by protected traits, and practical: buyers who discover they paid more than their neighbour feel cheated, and some stop buying.

And there is the collusion question of Part forty-four. In simulations by Emilio Calvano and coauthors, pricing algorithms that learned by trial and error settled on prices above the competitive level and punished undercutting, though nobody told them to collude. In August 2024 the Justice Department sued RealPage, whose software recommends rents to many landlords, alleging that pooling the landlords' private data through it raised rents. The legal question is old: what counts as an agreement. Prices set by the same software from the same pooled data are a new way of asking it.
B2B: Chapter thirteen. Business prices: negotiation, clauses, tenders.

Much of the economy's trade is between firms, and there the posted price is the exception. A supplier publishes a list price that almost nobody pays, and negotiates a discount with each customer. The discount is a bargain: Part eleven's split, landing between each side's alternative according to their bargaining power. So buyers of the same product pay different prices, by their size, their skill and how hard they push, and much of a pricing team's work is managing that dispersion. For large orders, buyers run tenders: sealed-bid auctions among suppliers, with the first-price rules of Part sixteen, and the bid-rigging screens of Part fifty-nine watching them.

One contract term deserves a closer look: the most-favoured-customer clause. A big customer insists that it will get any lower price the supplier gives anyone else. Without the clause, the supplier charges it 60 and a more price-sensitive customer 40. With it, any discount to the second customer must go to the first too, so the supplier charges both 50. The clause protects the buyer who has it by raising the price everyone else pays. Across sellers it can soften competition, since a seller who cuts its price for one customer must cut it for all. In 2013 a federal court found that Apple had conspired with publishers to raise the prices of e-books; clauses of this kind in their contracts were part of the story.
Dials: Chapter fourteen. The Dials: pass-through and elasticities.

This part opens one Dial and returns to another. The new one is cost pass-through to retail prices. American food, 2000 to 2019: 0.58 of a change in factory-gate prices reached the grocer's shelf within a year. 2021 to 2023: about 0.93, measured as the ratio of the two rises. And Staples' pass-through of a cost change at one firm only, from Part fifty-nine: about 0.16. The status is that it depends on the setting: on how much of the retail price is the retailer's own cost, and on whether rivals share the cost change. The same retailer passes on a shared shock far more than a private one.

The second Dial is Part forty-three's: how sensitive one product's sales are to its own price. Its rows from cars and cereal show the range, and the warning that an estimate below one in magnitude means the method has failed. This part adds DellaVigna and Gentzkow's stores: within the typical chain, from -2.81 to -2.22 between the tenth and ninetieth percentiles. A seventeen percent difference in the best prices, which the chains chose not to charge.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: pricing with learning.

The frontier joins the experiment to the price. A seller can charge any of six prices; the best, unknown to it, is 80 dollars. The classic approach tests every price on 1,200 customers, picks the winner, and commits. Its losses pile up during the test, and after it, whenever the test picked wrong, they keep growing. Thompson sampling, an idea from 1933, keeps a probability distribution over each price's chance of a sale, draws from it, and charges whichever price looks best in the draw. Prices that might be best keep being tried; prices that are clearly worse stop. Over twenty thousand customers it loses far less, and its losses grow ever more slowly. Pricing algorithms built on such bandits are now common online; the experiment and the price have become one activity, with chapter three's interference still to worry about.

What remains open? Pricing AI services, sold by usage, per token or per request, and by subscription tiers: the questions are this part's, versions, bundles and two-part tariffs, with costs that fall fast. Learning with many products, where a discount on one item moves another's sales, so items cannot be learned one at a time. Personalized prices with fairness constraints, limits on how far prices may differ between buyers. And learning sellers facing learning sellers, where the outcome may look like collusion with no one intending it. What remains hardest is that buyers learn too: a demand curve that a firm is busy learning can change because the firm is learning it.
